tickets.text: A tab's memory grows about 70-95 MB with each edit of a big slide, on #2597; the cause is not yet found. Found under #4, first in node: the editor's whole-program memos (Statics.mk, MakeTerm's three) kept the last 1000 programs, about 82 MB per edit of Full Body (local experiment 62aaaa28e4, branch memo-growth-experiment in ~/hazel-ci-heap). #2469's bounds (16 and 8 entries) were pushed to #2597 under #4 (5d576cc479). In the browser that is not the fix (2026-10-14, headless Chromium with precise memory and forced GC, Full Body, the shirt-width slider set 15 times, driver memo45.py kept in ~/.cache/hazel-diag): #2597's build c4e411f9c2 grows +1,388 MB (about 85-95 MB per edit); every whole-program memo at ONE entry, +1,101 MB, and each redraw 18-31 s instead of 2-7 s; the undo history capped at 2 (memos as pushed), +1,386 MB; both together, +1,093 MB (about 73 MB per edit; local commit d9eb3ba86d, branch undo2-test). So neither the memos nor the undo history keeps each edit. Ruled out by reading: EvalMetrics (small records, bounded). Next: two heap snapshots a few edits apart (Chromium's DevTools protocol) and the retainers of what grew. Suspects by reading: ProjectorView.ViewCache (never pruned; each entry pins a statics map, a dynamics map and an elaborated term; harmless only while projector ids stay the same), LivelitProj's tables, ProbeTargets, the worker client. Then the same check on #2635.

The recovering parser on a Livelit Playground slide: 452 s for full-body.hz. Found under #4: the editor's recovering parser (Parser.to_segment, segmented, but a slide is one long let ... in chain) is near-quadratic there. MenhirCorpus per file on a laptop: full-body 452 s, shoes 386, scenes 210, emotion-kids 178, witch 169; 2096 s for the playground, about 5 min of it when CI was green. ReparseDocSlides and TextRoundtrip.DocSlides parse the same slides again. If Matthew takes the gate (#4, local commit f953119482: over 25 KB, only in the weekly run), this is what brings them back per PR. Known leads from the 2026-09-28 profile: Insert.go per character re-molds the whole sibling run; Form.try_get is 12% (a cheap memo); GC 41%. Tried 2026-10-14 night: local commit 0825830190 (branch parser-get-base-memo in ~/hazel-ci-heap, on ci-heap-4-pick, not pushed) keeps each label's molds in Form.Molds.get_base and runs the atomic regexes once instead of up to three times. MenhirCorpus on eyes.hz, alternating runs: 90.1 and 84.6 s before, 75.4 and 72.5 s after, about 15% faster; the parse still matches Menhir and the quick suite passes. Not enough to drop the 25 KB gate (it would take the playground's 2096 s to about 1800); the per-character re-mold of the whole sibling run is the real cost.

The commit path: find which of the request's values are new (about 15 ms of hashing, profiled), and make the commit's redraw cheaper. Part done, 2026-10-14, in node on #2635 at 41897ec3a5 (probe 4f0e261652, branch request-hash-probe in ~/hazel-ci-heap-2635, local only): a release-like edit (one literal, ids kept) through the app's own path, six edits each, steady state. Statics after the edit (DefStatics, per item): 25–37 ms. Only about 5% of the request is new objects: Kids' Choice 2,039 of 40k program nodes and about 4,600 of 87k EvalInfo nodes; Full Body 396 of 196k and about 13,100 of 326k. Building the request: the EvalInfo projection is the largest part, 13–14 ms on Full Body and 2.5–9 ms on Kids' Choice, because project_from walks both whole statics maps in key order on every commit, though about 180 entries change; then hashing the new values about 1–4 ms, and encoding 1.5–5 ms. So the hashing is not the cost. Tried and dropped: keeping an entry that is equal by content (ValueHash) as well as by identity: Full Body's re-added entries 179 to 30 and its EvalInfo new nodes 13,100 to 2,200, but the whole request got slower (median about 20 ms against 17), since comparing by content hashes as much as it saves. Done and pushed to #2635, 2026-10-14: 043508921b (DefStatics hands EvalInfo the keys it touched; the projection updates only those) and 9fb2bdf067 (unchanged spine roots kept): on Full Body the request 15.5–18.8 → 2.5–3.0 ms, statics after the edit 25–31 → 16–20 ms. Carrying it to diverged branches is #47 (issue 013). The commit's redraw, the ticket's second half, is not started.
Measure the size of view samples on the wire (not trimmed as the result is) and the memory of the shared-value tables and per-object hashes.
Statics counts on dev: the analyses-per-expression counter and Test_StaticsPasses from #2635 (bd90642654, da3251d3e5), with a small corpus subset in the quick suite.
A budget on a slide: the evaluator's work after a figure move in the woods, where reuse failed before #2675.
Byte budgets: elaboration sizes on dev, and the worker's message sizes for a fixed interaction.
Ask the maintainers to require the test jobs for merging into dev: today no check is required, so a red budget is a signal, not a gate.
A timing report that informs and doesn't fail: base and head on one runner, repeated, phase by phase, perhaps from #2161's harness (David's call).

Option B from issue 005: evaluate each livelit's view in the worker, keep the last Html sent per livelit, and post patches to it, so view evaluation leaves the main thread. Needs the view runner (ViewCmdRunner) in the worker, a patch format, an element on the page that owns each livelit's DOM and applies patches, and handlers dispatched by id. Keep the page's own path for an interaction's immediate redraw, or every drag waits a round trip. Its condition is now met (2026-10-12, see #10): evaluating the view is about 69% of the main thread in a woods figure move, and C would save about 2%. Weigh it against making the view itself cheaper first (#1, #2).

Budgets harder to fool (issue 006's update, a count is not a time): count the call memo's own work (the nodes its keys put in form) and, if js_of_ocaml can report it, memory allocated, beside the evaluator's steps.

UX mode re-elaborates an open cell's item with fresh ids on every change (the drawn cell in issue 008's B), so its parts never match by hash and fall to the reuse check's slow path. Keep the ids stable when a cell is analyzed again.

The autosave in UX mode (save_current / persist_divided: the divided program printed to text and stored, 0.55 s profiled) landed inside a slider change in issue 008's B. With #6's fix the change ends first, so it no longer does, but it is still 0.55 s on the main thread about a second after every edit, where the next drag can meet it. Save when idle, or save only the changed cell.

Open cells draw their livelit views without the view memo (live_html, 449 ms per change profiled in issue 008's B with #6's fix), where the whole-program editor uses memo_view (163 ms in C). Give cells the memo. (Corrected 2026-10-12: B's 0.48 s of of_segment was the autosave printing text, not the cells' code views.)

Code-driven tests of the outline modes: a URL parameter (or test hook) that opens a slide in UX mode with chosen GUI rows, so a script reaches issue 008's B without clicking through the outline. Matthew: "let's consider that too with our UX feature".

Revise issue 008 to answer plainly: are conditions C (#2635, whole program) and B (UX mode, only the GUI) similar once the same fixes are applied to each? As written it confuses: the GUI-only view gives no responsiveness benefit, but with the fixes it is no loss either; say so up front. Re-measure B and C on #2635's current head (the reuse check's fix, the stream index, the has-type memo, the per-step changes all in), and add graphs in the issue itself, not just the thumbnail, taking issue 001's pictures as the model, especially in the short answers. 008 is published, so per the series' rules: a dated update box under the short answers, notes after superseded claims, and an Update section with the figures.

On Kids' Choice it was 8 of 104 ms (issue 001). It would also need a content hash as its key, since the woods' shapes are fresh objects each time, and handlers that find the current state at event time. The lever is evaluating the view: #1, #2, #18.

closed_tickets.text: Messed Up Dress Up: music by category, and transposing by interval. (1) Categories: a small number, about 8: reggae, house, groove, waltz, calypso, classic beats, and a few more of our choosing. Every category gets at least one song, a new one where none fits yet. The 17 tunes today could seed most of them: reggae (sunny reggae, bubble reggae, turtle steppers dub), calypso (beach calypso, beach soca jump-up, steel-pan lullaby), waltz (spooky waltz), and chases (tree-house, duck-pond, round-the-house); the rest to sort. The music picker becomes two chips: song category, then track. Classic beats gets three new funk / hip-hop instrumentals in the spirit of "Apache" (Incredible Bongo Band), about 3 minutes each, with sections that feature, in turn: bass guitar, bongo drums, drum kit (funk playing), organ, and rhythm and lead guitars, so each part can be heard on its own (and on the mixing board). Our own tunes in that style (breakbeat kit, bongos, organ, twangy guitar), not Apache's melody or its break. (2) Transpose by interval: next to the transpose slider (today ±24 half steps), three chips: minus | interval | plus. The interval chip cycles through every interval up to the octave: half step, whole step, minor 3rd, major 3rd, 4th, tritone, 5th, minor 6th, major 6th, minor 7th, major 7th, octave; the octave is the default. Minus and plus move the slider by exactly that interval. (3) The same per channel (each part on the mixing board): the three chips only, and in place of a slider an indicator of the channel's setting, none or −/+ X × the interval, where X counts the presses of minus or plus, up to 3. To settle while building: what the indicator shows if the interval chip changes between presses.
closed_tickets.outcome: Messed Up Dress Up 0.0.20, live (kids-choice-games 9cfa091, tag dress-up-0.0.20): music by kind (8 kinds, a kind row of chips then its tunes); three classic beats of our own, about 3 min each (bongo breakdown, canyon cruise, skatepark strut), every player in front in turn, six new instruments; ➖ | 🎵 interval | ➕ under the transpose slider (half step to octave, octave first) and on each pitched channel, up to 3 presses. Side quest ended at Matthew's word.

closed_tickets.text: Issue 009 of the series: fresh ids and lack of reuse. Hazel mints ids two ways: Id.mk, a gensym (counter + random bytes), and names derived from a parent (Id.derive, Id.next, IdTagged.fresh_deterministic, v5 UUIDs), the distinction of Incremental Computation with Names (Hammer et al., OOPSLA 2015). Measure what Hazel can tell us today: (1) elaboration: analyzing the same program twice, which nodes come back renamed, and how many enclosing parts then fail the reuse check's hash (issue 008's 122); (2) experiment: name those nodes deterministically, and what reuse it recovers; (3) evaluation: ids minted per evaluation, and whether re-evaluated values ever share ids (why the call memo erases them). MEASURED 2026-10-13 (node, #2635 c4e64060f1; harness ~/.cache/hazel-diag/Test_Names.re, experiments issue009_experiments.patch, uncommitted): (1) the same term analyzed twice (Statics.mk_unmemoized; the memoized mk returns the same object): Full Body 667 of 111,462 nodes renamed, all minted by statics, 692 expressions then differ by hash; Witch 798/844, Scenes 210/237, Polygons 14/23. Sources: UserLivelit.mk_expand_dot_def (each use's dispatch on def.expand, FreshGrammar), StaticsBase.fresh_ascription, and 85 nodes from the Drawing library. (2) naming the first two by their use / what they ascribe (Id.derive by path): 667 -> 85 renamed, 692 -> 247 hash-differing. After a slider edit, incremental reuse: names held 943 -> 1,002, renamed 105 -> 46, reused 336 either way (the structural fallback recovers it): names change the check's cost, not what is reused. (3) evaluation mints 461,422 ids for the woods picture (33,847 nodes); evaluated twice, equal in structure, not by hash; the only shared ids are the program's own. (4) THE WORKER'S RESPONSE DIFF (ShareCodec, keyed by ValueHash with ids; instrumented build on 8342, ~/.cache/hazel-diag/sharecodec_stats.patch + share_moves.py): 8 woods figure moves, slots sent vs if structure-equal parts were references: worker->page 387,625 vs 347,920 (1.11x), page->worker 43,248 vs 21,728 (1.99x, small: ~5,400 a move vs 749,480 at load). The diff works because incremental reuse returns the same objects (~2,900 refs a move): identity survives through reuse, not names. (5) TIMED, 5 runs: after a slider edit, incremental vs scratch (node, medians): Full Body 502 vs 451 ms, Witch 857 vs 791, Scenes 1,547 vs 1,571; named about the same. DRAFT issue 009 written 2026-10-13 (local commit in ~/hazel-perf-report, not pushed; generator ~/.cache/hazel-diag/gen009.py + body009.html). OPEN: identity memos with no structural fallback; Polygons' 13 hash-differing with nothing renamed.

closed_tickets.text: Merkle names at construction, then remeasure issue 009's derived-names experiment. 009: content-derived names took the woods' evaluation from 1.9 s to 44.2 s. Today Util.ValueHash is a LAZY Merkle hash: a walk on first use, remembered per object in a WeakMap; TypHash (#2661) remembers types' hashes per object; nothing is hashed as it is built, and environments and closures only as generic values. Fix: compute each node's content name when it is built, from its children's names (already known), an environment frame's from its parent's and its binding, a closure's from its environment and body: a few operations per allocation, never a walk (the paper's constant cost). A content name is separate from the provenance id a step's result keeps for probes, or two values from one piece of syntax would share a name. Steps: (1) profile the derived mode first, to find where the 23x goes (walks, the WeakMap and GC, fallbacks); (2) the construction-time names; (3) remeasure gensyms, names kept and time; (4) then finish issue 009's edits, including a CORRECTION: its claim that a hash that gives up is not remembered is wrong (ValueHash marks it unhashable, and a too-deep walk leaves objects marked busy for good). FOUND 2026-10-13: (a) the hashing is linear within an evaluation (each object walked once: 1,033,746 walked, 932,980 reused, the same every run); (b) but time per evaluation grew across a session (2.3 -> 5.5 -> 6.3 s; 44.2 s after a long run) with the same work and a growing heap: the side table (ValueHash's WeakMap). (c) Names kept ON each value (a hidden property, ~/.cache/hazel-diag/merkle_on_object.patch): flat, 2.2 / 2.5 / 2.2 s, about 1.4x fresh ids (1.6 s), names still kept (33,846 of 33,847). Full remeasure running.
closed_tickets.outcome: Matthew's hunch was right: the hashing was linear, but the side table it was kept in (ValueHash's WeakMap) made each evaluation slower than the last (2.3, 5.5, 6.3 s for the same work). Merkle names kept on the values (a hidden property, computed as a value is built) hold still (2.2, 2.5, 2.2 s) and cost 12 to 28% over fresh ids, not 23 times. Issue 009 updated: a section on it, two corrections, a theme-aware thumbnail. Experiment local: ~/.cache/hazel-diag/merkle_on_object.patch.
